tip: 'Der Verstorbene' is an adjective used as a noun, so it keeps adjective endings: 'dem Verstorbenen'.
'Sollen' means 'be supposed to' and pushes the main verb to the end as an infinitive: 'soll ... kontrollieren'.
After 'das', the adjective needs only a light '-e' ending: 'das kleine Kind'. The article already shows the gender, so the adjective stays simple.
Amount plus contents stand side by side with no word for 'of': 'eine Flasche Wein' = a bottle of wine.
'In' shows movement here, so it takes the accusative: 'in ein Café'. For a fixed location it would take the dative.
A stretch of time in the accusative needs no preposition: 'jeden Tag' = every day.
'Schlafen' changes its 'a' to 'ä' in the 'er/sie/es' form: 'sie schläft' = she sleeps.
Dative feminine ends in '-er': 'meiner Mutter' = to my mother, the person receiving what is shown.
'Vorbereiten' is separable, so the prefix 'vor' jumps to the end: 'bereite ich den Nachtisch vor'.
Genitive 'of the' uses 'des' for masculine and neuter nouns and adds '-s' to the noun: 'des Herbstlaubs' = of the autumn foliage.
'Aus' (from/out of) always takes the dative – no exceptions.
Start with 'Danach' and the verb still holds slot 2, so the subject drops in behind it: 'Danach räumen wir', not 'Danach wir räumen'.
'Sich treffen' needs a pronoun echoing the subject; 'uns' here means 'each other', as in 'wir treffen uns'.
After 'einen' the adjective takes '-en': 'einen großen Hund'. English leaves 'big' unchanged, but German bends the adjective to match.
In the perfect tense 'hat' holds slot 2 and 'geschrieben' waits at the very end: 'hat einen langen Brief an ihre Freundin geschrieben'.
The verb stays second no matter what comes first: front 'Am meisten' and 'vermisse' still lands in slot 2, pushing 'ich' behind it.
'Noch nie' means never once up to now, stronger than a plain 'nie': 'hat sich noch nie ... beschwert' says it has simply never happened.
German builds the most-often adverb as 'am' plus '-sten': 'Am häufigsten' means most frequently. There is no separate word like 'most'.
With a separable verb, 'zu' slips between the prefix and the stem: 'kennen' plus 'zu' plus 'lernen' becomes 'kennenzulernen'.
'Durch' always takes accusative.
Here 'freundlich' describes how you smile, so it acts as an adverb and takes no ending: 'lächelst so freundlich'.
'Etwas gut finden' means to like or approve of something, literally to find it good: 'findet die Idee gut'.
After 'ein' with a neuter noun, the adjective takes '-es': 'ein großes Herz'. 'Herz' is neuter.
'Kennen' means to be familiar with a thing or person; 'wissen' is for facts. A melody uses 'kenne'.
'Einen' is the accusative of 'ein' for masculine nouns.
Comparatives still take normal adjective endings: 'groß' becomes 'größer', then 'größeren' before 'Tisch'.
'Auf sich aufpassen' means to look after yourself; the prefix 'auf' moves to the end: 'pass auf dich auf'.
Accusative: 'sein' becomes 'seinen' for masculine – possessives follow the 'ein' pattern.
'Um den See herum': 'um' (around) always takes the accusative – 'den See', no exceptions.
A modal like 'muss' pushes the main verb to the very end as an infinitive: 'muss den Anker lichten'.
